goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35 — P1 confidence 75 — `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` — Ruby 2.0 lacks `String#scrub`, so every feed import reaching this line raises `NoMethodError`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that Ruby 2.0 lacks String#scrub method. Looking at the diff, the code `i.content.scrub` is called in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35. The String#scrub method was indeed introduced in Ruby 2.1, not Ruby 2.0. However, the diff doesn't show what Ruby version this project targets. Looking at the Gemfile and other files, there's no explicit Ruby version constraint visible in the diff. The finding makes an assumption about the Ruby version being 2.0, but this is speculation - the project could be targeting Ruby 2.1+ where scrub is available. Without evidence in the diff that Ruby 2.0 is the target version, this finding is speculative about the runtime environment rather than a verifiable problem in the code itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/views/embed/loading.html.erb:7 — P2 confidence 75 — `document.location.reload();` — The loading flow has no terminal failure or timeout state, so a permanently failed retrieval reloads forever without an actionable error.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the loading.html.erb has a 30-second reload loop with no terminal failure state. Looking at the code flow: when no topic_id is found, the embed controller enqueues a RetrieveTopic job and renders 'loading', which then reloads after 30 seconds. If the retrieval permanently fails (e.g., invalid URL, network issues, missing user), the page will keep reloading indefinitely. However, this is more of a UX/design concern than a bug - the system is designed to poll until content is available. The retrieval has throttling (60 seconds in topic_retriever.rb) and will eventually succeed or the user will navigate away. While not ideal UX, this is a deliberate design choice for an async loading pattern, not a clear defect. The code works as intended - it's a polling mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 — P2 confidence 100 — `create_table :top_topics, force: true do |t|` — The embed/feed-import change modifies an unrelated historical migration, creating untraceable scope drift and potentially dropping an existing table.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb was modified to add 'force: true' to the create_table call. This is a real problem because adding 'force: true' to a migration means it will drop the table if it already exists before creating it. For a historical migration that may have already run in production, this change could cause data loss if the migration is ever re-run. The change appears unrelated to the main feature being added (embedding/feed importing) and modifies migration behavior in a potentially destructive way.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:116 — P1 confidence 100 — `method_option :strip, aliases: '-s', required: false, desc: "Text to strip from titles"` — Removing the formerly supported `--category/-c` option silently breaks the importer CLI contract and forces imported topics out of their requested category.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the `--category/-c` option was indeed removed from the disqus.thor import task. The old code had `method_option :category, aliases: '-c', desc: 'The category to post in'` and used it to set `category_id` when creating posts via `PostCreator.new(user, title: t[:title], raw: ..., category: category_id)`. The new code removes this option entirely and switches to using `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])` which doesn't accept a category parameter. This is a real breaking change - users who previously used `--category` to import Disqus threads into specific categories will now have their imports go to the default category instead, and the CLI option is silently removed rather than deprecated with a warning.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:41 — P1 confidence 75 — `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` — One missing embed synchronously imports the entire feed, making every cache miss an unbounded network/parse/database batch whose failure prevents direct retrieval fallback.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in lib/topic_retriever.rb:41, when `perform_retrieve` is called and the embed URL is not found, it checks if feed_polling_enabled and then calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` synchronously. This is a valid concern - the PollFeed job fetches an RSS feed, parses it, and imports all items. This happens synchronously during a web request (triggered from EmbedController#best which calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic), but the job itself runs synchronously when called via execute). However, looking more carefully, the RetrieveTopic job is enqueued asynchronously via `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` in embed_controller.rb:14, so this runs in a background job, not blocking the web request. The finding's concern about 'every cache miss' causing unbounded work is valid - if feed polling is enabled, a single missing embed triggers importing the entire feed. This is a real architectural issue where one user's request can trigger significant background work, and if the feed import fails, the fallback to fetch_http still runs. The concern about failure preventing fallback is incorrect though - the code continues to fetch_http after the poll regardless of success.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:36 — P1 confidence 75 — `revisor.revise!(user, absolutize_urls(url, contents), skip_validations: true, bypass_rate_limiter: true)` — The post revision and later content-hash update are not transactional or success-checked, so a failed save can still suppress all retries.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 30-37, when updating an existing embed: `revisor.revise!` is called, and then `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` is called separately. These two operations are not wrapped in a transaction. If `revise!` succeeds but `update_column` fails (or vice versa), the data could be in an inconsistent state. However, the finding claims 'a failed save can still suppress all retries' - this is somewhat speculative. The `revise!` method returns a boolean but it's not checked here. If the revision fails, the content_sha1 would still be updated, meaning future imports would think the content is already up-to-date and skip the update. This is a real consistency issue - if revise! fails but update_column succeeds, the embed record shows the new hash but the post wasn't actually updated, and future attempts won't retry because the hash matches.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:4 — P2 confidence 100 — `t.integer :topic_id, null: false` — The unconstrained topic identifier has no foreign key, so deletion or bad writes can leave an embed pointing to a nonexistent topic.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points out that the topic_embeds table has a topic_id column without a foreign key constraint to the topics table. Looking at the migration in db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb, it creates `t.integer :topic_id, null: false` but does not add a foreign key constraint. This is a valid observation about database design - without a foreign key, referential integrity is not enforced at the database level, meaning topic_embeds records could reference non-existent topics if topics are deleted. However, this is more of a database design best practice/style issue rather than a clear bug. Rails applications commonly rely on application-level validations (like `belongs_to :topic` in the model) rather than database-level foreign keys. The code would still function correctly - it's just missing an additional layer of data integrity protection. This is a design choice rather than a defect that would cause incorrect behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:5 — P2 confidence 100 — `t.integer :post_id, null: false` — The unconstrained post identifier has no foreign key, permitting orphaned embeds that break the update path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that the lack of a foreign key constraint on post_id permits orphaned embeds. Looking at the migration, it creates a topic_embeds table with post_id as NOT NULL but without a foreign key constraint. However, this is a design choice common in Rails applications where referential integrity is often handled at the application level rather than database level. The TopicEmbed model has 'belongs_to :post' which provides application-level association. While adding a foreign key would be better for data integrity, the absence of one is not a bug or defect - it's a common Rails pattern. The code will function correctly; orphaned records would only occur if posts are deleted without cleaning up embeds, which is a separate concern. This is more of a best practice suggestion than a real defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:35 — P1 confidence 100 — `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` — Untrusted feed HTML is imported with raw HTML rendering and validation bypassed, enabling persistent XSS in the same-origin embed iframe.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real security issue. Looking at the code flow: 1) In poll_feed.rb:35, content from RSS feed is processed with `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` and passed to `TopicEmbed.import()`. 2) In topic_embed.rb:21, `PostCreator.new()` is called with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`. 3) In post.rb:131-133, when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, the `cook` method returns `raw` directly without any sanitization. 4) This raw HTML is then rendered in embed/best.html.erb:17 with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. The embed iframe runs on the same origin as Discourse (it's served from the Discourse domain), so any JavaScript in the imported content would execute with full access to the Discourse session. This is a legitimate persistent XSS vulnerability where untrusted RSS feed content is rendered as raw HTML without sanitization.

adjudication_records.issue_text:
app/models/topic_embed.rb:13 — P1 confidence 75 — `contents << "\\n
\\n#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")}\\n"` — An attacker-controlled embed URL is interpolated unescaped into an HTML attribute and body, enabling persistent markup or script injection.

adjudication.rationale:
Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb:13, the `url` parameter is interpolated directly into HTML without escaping: `contents << "
#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")} "`. The URL comes from external sources (RSS feeds in poll_feed.rb line 32-33 where `url = i.link` or `url = i.id`, and from embed_url parameter in embed_controller.rb). While there is a check `return unless url =~ /^https?\:///` on line 11, this only validates the URL starts with http:// or https://, but doesn't prevent XSS payloads like `http://evil.com/">`. An attacker could craft a malicious URL in an RSS feed that would be stored and rendered without escaping, leading to persistent XSS when the content is displayed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — P1 confidence 75 — `doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read,` — Hostname-only validation does not constrain resolved IPs or redirects, allowing DNS rebinding or redirects to reach loopback and private services.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in TopicEmbed.import_remote. The code at line 48 uses `open(url).read` to fetch content from a user-controlled URL. While there is hostname validation in TopicRetriever.invalid_host? that checks if the URL's host matches SiteSetting.embeddable_host, this validation is insufficient because: 1) DNS rebinding attacks can cause the hostname to resolve to internal IPs after validation, 2) HTTP redirects from the allowed host could redirect to internal services, 3) The validation only checks the hostname string, not the actual resolved IP address. The open() call will follow redirects and connect to whatever IP the DNS resolves to, potentially allowing access to internal services like localhost, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata), or private network resources. This is a real SSRF vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:10 — P2 confidence 100 — `response.should_not be_success` — The test claims a 404 but accepts any failure status, so an unrelated 500 response passes.

adjudication.rationale: The test at line 10 checks 'response.should_not be_success' after calling 'get :best' without an embed_url parameter. The finding claims this is problematic because it 'accepts any failure status' when the test 'claims a 404'. However, looking at the test code, the comment says 'it is 404 without an embed_url' but the actual assertion only checks that the response is not successful. This is actually a valid test pattern - it's testing that the endpoint fails without required parameters. The comment '404' is just descriptive context, not a strict requirement. The test correctly verifies the endpoint doesn't succeed without required params. Additionally, looking at the controller code, it uses 'params.require(:embed_url)' which would raise an ActionController::ParameterMissing exception (typically resulting in a 400 Bad Request), not a 404. So the comment is slightly misleading, but the test assertion itself is reasonable - it's checking that the request fails. This is a minor documentation/comment accuracy issue at most, not a real bug in the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:43 — P1 confidence 100 — `TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever)` — The test asserts synchronous retrieval while the controller enqueues a job, so it tests a nonexistent path and misses the actual job contract.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the controller code in embed_controller.rb, when topic_id is nil, it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` which is an asynchronous job enqueue. However, the test in spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:43 sets up `TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever)` and `retriever.expects(:retrieve)`, expecting TopicRetriever to be called directly. But the controller actually enqueues a job via `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`, not calling TopicRetriever directly. The TopicRetriever is called inside the job (in app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb), not in the controller. So the test is mocking something that doesn't happen in the controller action - it's testing a code path that doesn't exist. The test would pass because the mock expectations aren't verified properly (expects(:new).returns(retriever) would never be called, but mocha might not fail on unmet expectations depending on configuration). This is a real test defect.

adjudication.rationale: The finding criticizes the test for mocking internal methods like `retrieved_recently?` and `perform_retrieve`, arguing this reduces test coverage. However, this is a legitimate unit testing approach - the test is specifically testing the `retrieve` method's behavior based on different conditions. The test file does test the throttle logic indirectly by testing that `perform_retrieve` is called or not called based on `retrieved_recently?`. This is a style/testing philosophy concern rather than a real bug or defect in the code. The actual Redis throttle implementation exists in the production code and could be tested separately. This is not a correctness problem or bug - it's a subjective opinion about test design.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 — P1 confidence 75 — `create_table :top_topics, force: true do |t|` — Changing the historical migration to force creation drops a pre-existing table and its data instead of failing safely on schema conflict.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb, the migration was changed from `create_table :top_topics do |t|` to `create_table :top_topics, force: true do |t|`. Adding `force: true` to a migration means that if the table already exists, it will be dropped and recreated, which would destroy any existing data. This is a real problem because migrations are meant to be run sequentially and should be idempotent in a safe way - they shouldn't destroy data if run in an environment where the table might already exist. However, looking at the context, this appears to be a new migration file being created (the file path shows it's being added), so the `force: true` would only be problematic if someone had already run a previous version of this migration or if the table existed from another source. The finding correctly identifies that this is a potentially dangerous change to migration behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:3 — P1 confidence 75 — `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true do |t|` — The new migration silently drops a pre-existing same-named table, making deployment destructive and unrecoverable instead of surfacing the conflict.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that using `force: true` in the migration is dangerous because it silently drops a pre-existing table. Looking at the diff, the migration at db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb does use `create_table :topic_embeds, force: true`. This is a new table being created for a new feature (topic embeds). The `force: true` option would drop the table if it already exists before creating it. However, this is a new migration for a new feature - the topic_embeds table shouldn't exist before this migration runs. The `force: true` is commonly used to ensure idempotency during development but is indeed risky in production migrations. However, looking at the context, this appears to be a legitimate concern - if someone had manually created this table or if the migration was run partially, using `force: true` would silently destroy data. This is a real issue that could cause data loss in edge cases, though the severity depends on deployment practices.
